explanations.answer: Once all the flocks are gathered there
explanations.explanation: That's the well's rule. When all the flocks have been gathered, the shepherds roll the stone away, water the sheep, and put the stone back over the mouth of the well (Genesis 29:3). It's like waiting for the whole batch to cool before anybody touches a cookie. Nobody gets a head start.

One flock isn't enough to open this well. The text says the shepherds wait until all the flocks have been gathered (Genesis 29:3). Three flocks are already lying near it when Jacob shows up, and the stone still stays put.

explanations.answer: Once each shepherd pays the owner
explanations.explanation: Payment never comes up at this well, friend. The text says the shepherds roll the stone away once all the flocks have been gathered, then water the sheep (Genesis 29:3). No fee in sight. Just a big stone and a lot of waiting.

Jacob asks, "where are you from?" and they answer, "We are from Haran…" (Genesis 29:4) That's the very place Jacob was headed when he left Beersheba (Genesis 28:10). He asked a stranger one simple question and landed right on target.

Bethel is the place Jacob named after his dream on the road (Genesis 28:19). The shepherds don't say that, though. They tell Jacob, "We are from Haran…" (Genesis 29:4) So the town he was looking for is the one they come from.

Beersheba is where Jacob started out. He left it to head for Haran (Genesis 28:10). The shepherds at the well say, "We are from Haran…" (Genesis 29:4) I think Jacob's heart skipped a beat when he heard it.

Careful, friend, that one is False. When Jacob asks if they know Laban the grandson of Nahor, the shepherds answer, “We know him…” (Genesis 29:5). Then Jacob asks, “Is he well?” and they say, “Yes,” and point out that Laban's daughter Rachel is coming with his sheep (Genesis 29:6). Jacob asked one little question and got good news AND Rachel walking up. That's a bonus nobody ordered!
Right, they know him. Jacob asks about Laban the grandson of Nahor, and they say, “We know him…” (Genesis 29:5). Then they tell Jacob Laban is well. I bet Jacob was smiling by then.

Rachel is Laban's daughter, and the shepherds say she's coming with his sheep (Genesis 29:6). She is also a shepherdess, so those sheep are hers to look after (Genesis 29:9). Keep that name in your pocket, friend.
Milcah shows up in Genesis, but she's Nahor's wife (Genesis 11:29). The shepherds point to Laban's daughter, and her name is Rachel (Genesis 29:6). Easy name to mix up in a crowd of Bible names.

Deborah is a name from Rebekah's household, where she was Rebekah's nurse (Genesis 35:8). The one walking up to the well with Laban's sheep is a different person. The shepherds say it's his daughter Rachel (Genesis 29:6).

explanations.answer: Water the sheep and take them back to pasture
explanations.explanation: That's what Jacob says. It's still broad daylight, so he tells the shepherds to water the sheep and take them back to pasture (Genesis 29:7). Brand new in town and already giving orders at the well. Confidence, friend.

explanations.answer: Bring the sheep home and shut them in
explanations.explanation: Jacob never says anything about going home or shutting the sheep in. He says it's not yet time to gather the livestock, so they should water the sheep and take them back to pasture (Genesis 29:7). He wants them out working while the daylight lasts.

explanations.answer: Let the sheep rest by the well till dark
explanations.explanation: Resting till dark isn't what Jacob says. Since it's still broad daylight, he tells the shepherds to water the sheep and take them back to pasture (Genesis 29:7). I think he's looking at those sheep lying around and thinking they should be doing something.

He sure does. As soon as Jacob sees Rachel with Laban's sheep, he goes up, rolls the stone away from the mouth of the well, and waters his uncle's sheep (Genesis 29:10). Just before this, the shepherds told him, “We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away…” (Genesis 29:8). Then Jacob walks up and rolls it himself, like that stone owed him money!

It's true, he does it himself. The text says that as soon as Jacob saw Rachel with Laban's sheep, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well (Genesis 29:10). Then he watered his uncle's sheep. Whew. I'd want a nap after moving that stone.
That's exactly what she does. Jacob tells her he's Rebekah's son and a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father (Genesis 29:12). She didn't walk. Good news travels fast, friend.

explanations.answer: Asks him to wait by the well
explanations.explanation: Nope, no asking him to wait in this story, friend. Once Jacob tells her he's Rebekah's son and a relative of her father, the text says she ran and told her father (Genesis 29:12). Ran! If somebody told me a relative of my father was standing at the well, I'd be moving too. I'd trip over my own apron, but I'd be moving.

explanations.answer: Sends a shepherd to fetch Laban
explanations.explanation: Rachel doesn't send anybody. The text says she ran and told her father herself (Genesis 29:12). She carries the news with her own two feet.

Laban doesn't wait at all. When he heard the news about his sister's son Jacob, he ran out to meet him (Genesis 29:13). Then he embraced him, kissed him, and brought him to his home. The man RAN, friend.
Right, he doesn't wait. Laban heard the news about his sister's son Jacob and ran out to meet him (Genesis 29:13). He embraced him, kissed him, and brought him home. Nobody had to knock on his door.

That's what Laban says. After Jacob has told him all that had happened, Laban declares, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.” (Genesis 29:14) Jacob is Laban's sister's son, so it fits. I think that was a warm welcome for a traveler who'd come a long way.
He does say it. Laban declares, “You are indeed my own flesh and blood.” (Genesis 29:14) Jacob is his sister's son. That's family talking, friend.
Laban says, "Tell me what your wages should be." (Genesis 29:15) He doesn't want his relative working for nothing. So Jacob gets to name his own price. That's a generous opening offer.

Duties sound like a job description, but that's not what Laban asks for. He says, "Tell me what your wages should be." (Genesis 29:15) He wants Jacob to name his pay. Duties never paid anybody's bills, friend. A wage is the part where the work gets paid back.
No fancy title is on the table here. Laban asks Jacob, "Tell me what your wages should be." (Genesis 29:15) He's talking about pay, not a job name on a door.
It's the other way around. The text says the older daughter is Leah, and the younger is Rachel (Genesis 29:16). Hold on to that order. It matters later in this passage.

Right, Rachel is the younger one. Laban's older daughter is Leah, and the younger is Rachel (Genesis 29:16). Leah first, Rachel second. Write it on your oven mitt, friend, because that order is about to matter.

Jacob says, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." (Genesis 29:18) The text tells us he offers it because he loves her. Seven years is a long time to sign up for. That tells you where his heart is.

Two years is a lot less than what Jacob offers. He says, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." (Genesis 29:18) The text says he offers it because he loves her. He wasn't haggling.

Five is a nice round number, but it's not Jacob's. He says, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." (Genesis 29:18) Seven. That's a lot of batches, friend, and the text says he made the offer because he loves her.

explanations.answer: It's better than giving her to another
explanations.explanation: That's Laban's reply. Jacob offers seven years for Rachel, and Laban says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) Notice he doesn't haggle or ask for more. He just says yes and tells Jacob to stay. Fastest deal in the whole passage, and the shortest seven-year contract negotiation ever!

explanations.answer: Jacob must ask his father Isaac first
explanations.explanation: Isaac doesn't come up in Laban's reply, friend. Laban says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) No stopping to make a call, no "let me get back to you." Laban says it's better to give Rachel to Jacob than to another, and then he tells Jacob to stay. I think Laban had made up his mind.

explanations.answer: Rachel has to agree to it first
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Laban say anything about Rachel agreeing. He says, “Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me.” (Genesis 29:19) It's Laban who answers Jacob, and that's all we're told.

The text says Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her (Genesis 29:20). Love changed how the time felt. Seven years like a few days is not how a Monday morning feels, friend.

That's how a long wait usually feels, but it's not what the text says. It says Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her (Genesis 29:20). His love made the time fly.
The text goes the other direction. It says that for Jacob the seven years seemed but a few days because of his love for her (Genesis 29:20). Love made them feel short, not long.
It didn't go that way. When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob (Genesis 29:23). Leah is Laban's older daughter. Hang on to that, because this is a big turn.

That's right. When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob (Genesis 29:23). Jacob had served seven years for Rachel, and the evening ended with Leah. This is a big turn in the story.
That's the word Jacob uses. He asks Laban, “Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25) He had served seven years for Rachel. I think that morning hit him hard.
Jacob doesn't say Laban rushed him. He says, “Wasn’t it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25) His complaint is that he was deceived, not hurried.
Jacob doesn't say anything about being forgotten. He asks, “Why have you deceived me?” (Genesis 29:25) He says it right after he realizes it was Leah, not Rachel.

explanations.answer: Marrying off the younger daughter before the older
explanations.explanation: That's the custom Laban names. He says, “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.” (Genesis 29:26) Leah is the older daughter and Rachel is the younger (Genesis 29:16). That's the reason he gives Jacob.

explanations.answer: Holding a wedding feast for a relative from far away
explanations.explanation: The feast isn't what Laban points to. He had invited all the men of that place and prepared one himself (Genesis 29:22). His custom is about the order of his daughters: “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.” (Genesis 29:26)

explanations.answer: Letting a groom work off the price of his bride
explanations.explanation: Laban doesn't object to Jacob's work. He had accepted the seven years himself when Jacob offered them (Genesis 29:18 to 19). The custom he names is this: “It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.” (Genesis 29:26)

That's the price. Laban says to finish the week's celebration, and they will give him the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). That's seven more on top of the seven he's already put in. A long road for Jacob.
Silver isn't mentioned. Laban says they will give Jacob the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). The payment is work, same as before.

Isaac's flocks never come up here, friend. Laban says they will give Jacob the younger one in return for another seven years of work (Genesis 29:27). What Laban asks for is more of Jacob's work. Seven years was already a long stretch, and now he asks for seven more. I'd need a bigger calendar.

He doesn't turn it down. The text says Jacob did just that: he finished the week's celebration, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29:28). Nothing in the text has him heading home. I think that says a lot about how he felt about Rachel.

Right, he stays. Jacob finishes the week's celebration, and Laban gives him Rachel as his wife (Genesis 29:28). Then the text says he worked for Laban another seven years (Genesis 29:30). Nobody packs a bag in this passage, friend. Seven more years is a LONG time to wait, and I think that tells you how much he loved her.
The text says it plainly: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah (Genesis 29:30). That's how it is in this house. I think this is a tender spot, and Leah's part of the story isn't finished.
The text says otherwise. Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah (Genesis 29:30). I think this one hurts a little. Take it slow with this part, friend.
